answers.question: The race got moved two weeks earlier, to October 18, because of the bridge works. That's three weeks from today. I've only done one 20. Do I still have time for my 22-miler?
answers.answer:
No, skip the 22. With the race three weeks away, a 22 would add fatigue you will not fully recover from before Oct 18.

Your 20 on Sep 13 and 17 on Sep 27 already give you the endurance. Sunday's 18 miles, with the last 4 at marathon pace, is the longest run that fits the final weeks.

new.analysis:
## What happened last week
Last week went to plan. All five runs matched their planned distances, both rest days were taken, and nothing was added or cut.

The quality session was 9 miles with three 2-mile reps. They averaged 7:58 per mile against a target of 8:00, and the pace faded only 1 percent across the reps. Heart rate climbed about 19 beats over the session, which is normal for a hard effort in warm conditions.

The 17-mile long run averaged 9:59 per mile with even splits. The last three miles were no faster than the rest, so the pace was controlled, and heart rate drifted only 4.7 beats.

The easy share came in at 61 percent, under the 80 percent target. The easy runs themselves sat at 138 to 139 beats, which is solid zone 2, so the gap comes from the quality session and the zone 3 time on the long run.

## Why this week looks like this
Race-specific work now moves from threshold to marathon pace. Threshold builds the engine, but with the race three weeks away the goal is to rehearse your goal pace on fresh legs and on tired legs.

| Pace | Per mile | Where it shows up this week |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Easy runs | 9:50 | Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday |
| Long run | 9:59 | Sunday, last 12 miles |
| Marathon pace | 8:30 to 8:45 | Wednesday reps, last 4 miles Sunday |
| Under 3:45 goal | 8:35 | The average you need over 26.2 miles |

The Thursday run becomes a medium-long run of 8 miles. It adds time on feet in the middle of the week without making the weekend a second hard session. Volume rises from 42 to 45 miles, about 7 percent, which is enough to keep the work building without tipping into fatigue this close to the race.

The Sunday long run stays at 18 miles and finishes with 4 miles at race pace. That keeps the run near 2 hours 53 minutes, inside the 2.5 to 3 hour range, and avoids a 22 that would cost more recovery than it adds.

## Is the goal realistic
Under 3:45 needs 8:35 per mile for the full 26.2 miles. That is about 84 seconds per mile faster than your long-run pace, so the gap is real. Your threshold reps show you can hold near 8 minutes per mile for two miles, which is encouraging, but four miles at marathon pace on Sunday is the real test. Use what those miles tell you to set the race-day target, and be ready to hold effort steady rather than chase the number early.
